doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Digital downloads and remembering record stores in Philadelphia
summary: Dorn accepts digital downloads while missing album covers. He remembers buying mono records at Riles and listening in the Paramount Record Shop.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What do you think about the digital downloading business?

What am I going to do, tell you I wish albums were here so the covers were big and I could read Nat’s liner notes? It’s what it is. So now I make — I don’t care if somebody buys it by clicking their heels together and wishing for it to come through the ether. However you’re selling stuff is how you sell stuff. It’s fine. I mean listen, there were guys who probably hand made horse and buggies that were breathtakingly well done and well crafted and sturdy and everything. But when the car came along that movie was over. I didn’t like it when it went from albums to CDs because it changed, number one, the sound of the music. I like the sound of vinyl. And I also miss a cover that’s this big. You can look at and then you flip it over and the notes are in there, if it’s a fold-out you get page — you know? There was something about holding an album in your hand —
Plus you could stand in the store and read the backs of them.

Oh man, I mean see, when I was a kid I used to allow myself one mono record a week, because I was working in high school to save money to go to college, right? So when I got my paycheck on Friday I would go to a record store in Upper Darby which was the town next to the town I lived in, Yeadon, which is right outside of Philly, Riles Record Store, and then I would, for my $1.98 mono record, I’d look at five thousand records before I made my choice. What was it going to be? And there was something about that that just felt good. You’d hold a record, you’d look at it, you’d flip it over, you’d go in

there and you’d find out a new record came out you weren’t aware of, and they would play them for me. The guy and his wife that owned that store were so nice to me. They would play it. And there used to be a place in South Philly called Paramount Record Shop, it was one of the few black owned record shops in the city, a guy named Felix owned it. And I would come in on a Saturday afternoon and they’d say oh here comes the white boy again. And I’d listen. And I’d say well can you play me — so finally they just like said listen, don’t scratch anything, go into the booth, listen to whatever you want. So I would listen to Mahalia Jackson or I would listen to The Five Satins or I’d listen to The Penguins, or whatever the records were. It was — Clara Ward. Only — records you could only get there. Stuff on Atlantic, stuff on King. It was just a different time. So I miss all of that. But the thing that makes me not turn into a blithering idiot is that I had that experience. So now is now. I make a record, whatever you want to release it on, however you want to sell it, that’s your business. I’m just interesting in making the music.
